subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Sunspots and the Solar Cycle
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Sunspots and the Solar Cycle.

hook.text: Dark blotches appear on the Sun's surface, grow, then fade. They follow an 11-year rhythm.

buildup.text: Sunspots are cooler regions caused by intense magnetic activity. They can be larger than Earth.

discovery.text: Galileo observed them through a telescope in 1612, proving the Sun is not a perfect, unchanging sphere.

twist.text: From 1645 to 1715, sunspots nearly vanished. Europe froze. The link to climate is still debated.

climax.text: At solar maximum, sunspots peak and flares surge. At solar minimum, the Sun goes quiet for years.

punchline.text: Even stars have moods on an 11-year clock.

quiz.question: What did the disappearance of sunspots from 1645 to 1715 coincide with?
options: A period of unusually cold temperatures in Europe
A dramatic increase in solar flare activity
The discovery of new planets in the solar system

details.summary: Sunspots are cooler, darker regions on the Sun's surface caused by intense magnetic fields that inhibit convection. They wax and wane in an approximately 11-year solar cycle, during which the Sun's magnetic field flips polarity.
details.whyItMatters: The solar cycle affects Earth's space weather environment, satellite operations, and even subtle climate variations. Predicting cycle intensity helps protect astronauts, power grids, and global communications infrastructure.
takeaways: Sunspots are magnetically cooled darker regions on the Sun's surface
They follow an approximately 11-year activity cycle
More sunspots correlate with more flares and space weather events

faq.question: Why are sunspots cooler than the surrounding surface?
faq.answer: Strong magnetic fields (thousands of times Earth's) suppress convection — the rising of hot gas from below. With convection inhibited, the sunspot region is about 3,800°C versus the surrounding 5,500°C. They appear dark only by contrast; a sunspot alone would still be blindingly bright.

faq.question: Can the solar cycle affect Earth's climate?
faq.answer: Slightly. Total solar energy output varies by about 0.1% over the cycle, which alone is too small for significant climate change. However, prolonged low-activity periods (like the Maunder Minimum, 1645-1715) may have contributed to cooler temperatures.
